The Website Redesign Checklist for Home Service Businesses [40-Point Checklist]

Complete 40-point website redesign checklist for home service businesses. Includes planning, design, development, launch, and post-launch.

If your plumbing, HVAC, roofing, or electrical business website is stuck in 2018 — slow, clunky, and bleeding mobile leads — this is the only guide you need. We have redesigned 200+ contractor websites and distilled every critical step into a 40-point checklist. Follow it, and you will avoid the $15,000+ mistakes we see home service businesses make every month.

Why Most Contractor Website Redesigns Fail (And How This Checklist Fixes That)

Here is a number that should keep you up at night: 38% of visitors stop engaging with a website if the layout is unattractive, according to Adobe's State of Content report. For home service contractors, that is not just a lost visitor — that is a $3,000 HVAC install or a $12,000 roof replacement walking out the digital door.

We have audited hundreds of contractor websites at OnwardCraft. The pattern is always the same. A business owner hires a generalist web designer who has never worked with a service company. The designer builds something pretty but functionally broken. No local SEO foundation. No conversion path. No mobile optimization. The site launches, traffic drops, and the owner assumes "websites just don't work for my industry."

That assumption costs contractors millions in lost revenue annually. The problem is not that websites don't work for home services. The problem is that most website redesign steps skip the parts that actually drive calls and form submissions.

The Real Cost of a Bad Redesign

A poorly executed contractor website redesign checklist costs you in three ways:

  • Direct costs: $5,000–$25,000 spent on design and development that produces zero ROI
  • Opportunity costs: 6–12 months of lost leads while you fix what should have been done right the first time
  • SEO damage: Rankings tank when URLs change without proper redirects, costing you organic traffic you spent years building

One HVAC client came to us after a redesign dropped their organic traffic 64% in 90 days. Their previous agency changed every URL, removed location pages, and built the new site on a slow page builder. It took us eight months and $18,000 in recovery work to get them back to where they started. That is why this website redesign process exists — to prevent exactly that scenario.

What Makes This Checklist Different

Most website redesign checklists online are written by generic marketing blogs. They tell you to "define your goals" and "choose a color scheme" without explaining what a home service business actually needs. This checklist is different because it is built from 200+ contractor redesigns across plumbing, HVAC, roofing, electrical, pest control, and landscaping.

Every point on this list has been battle-tested. Every recommendation comes from a real mistake we have seen cost a contractor money. And every phase is designed to move a visitor from "just browsing" to "calling for a quote" as fast as possible.

Phase 1: Planning (Points 1–10) — The Foundation That Determines Everything

Short answer: The planning phase of a website redesign involves auditing your current site, defining measurable goals, analyzing competitors, mapping your customer journey, documenting existing assets, setting a realistic budget and timeline, assembling your team, choosing your platform, planning your content, and establishing your measurement framework. Skip any of these, and your redesign is built on sand.

After managing 200+ contractor redesigns, we can say with absolute certainty: planning determines 70% of your redesign success. The contractors who spend two weeks in planning launch faster, rank higher, and convert better than those who rush to design. Here is your 10-point planning checklist.

Point 1: Audit Your Current Website Performance

Before you change a single pixel, you need to know what is working and what is not. We start every redesign with a comprehensive audit covering:

  • Traffic sources: Where do your visitors come from? Organic search, Google Ads, direct, referral?
  • Top-performing pages: Which pages drive the most calls and form submissions?
  • Conversion rates: What percentage of visitors contact you? Industry average for home services is 2–5%.
  • Page speed: Use Google PageSpeed Insights. Anything below 70 on mobile needs fixing.
  • Current keyword rankings: Document every page 1 ranking you have. You will protect these during the redesign.

One roofing contractor we worked with in Dallas discovered that 40% of their leads came from a single blog post about "hail damage roof repair." Without the audit, they might have deleted that post during the redesign. Instead, we made it a cornerstone page and increased its traffic 180%.

Point 2: Define Specific, Measurable Goals

"We want a better website" is not a goal. "Increase form submissions 40% in 90 days" is. Every goal in your website redesign checklist should be SMART:

Bad Goal Good Goal How to Measure
Get more traffic Increase organic traffic 30% in 6 months Google Analytics 4 sessions
Look more professional Reduce bounce rate from 75% to 55% GA4 engagement rate
Get more leads Increase conversion rate from 2% to 4% Form submissions + calls via call tracking
Rank better on Google Rank top 3 for 10 target keywords in 90 days SEMrush or Ahrefs position tracking

Point 3: Analyze Your Top 3 Competitors

Do not copy your competitors. Study them to find gaps you can exploit. For each competitor, document:

  1. Their top 5 ranking pages (use Ahrefs or SEMrush)
  2. Their call-to-action strategy — where do they place "Get a Quote" buttons?
  3. Their service area coverage — which cities do they target?
  4. Their review count and average rating on Google
  5. Their page load speed (use GTmetrix)

A plumbing client in Phoenix discovered their biggest competitor had no dedicated page for "tankless water heater installation." We built one, optimized it, and that page alone generated $47,000 in new business in its first year.

Point 4: Map Your Customer Journey

Home service customers move through distinct stages. Your website redesign steps must address each one:

  • Awareness: "My AC is making a weird noise" — they need educational content
  • Consideration: "Should I repair or replace my AC?" — they need comparison guides
  • Decision: "Who should I hire?" — they need trust signals and easy contact options
  • Post-purchase: "How do I maintain this?" — they need follow-up content that drives reviews and referrals

Point 5: Inventory Your Existing Content and Assets

Create a spreadsheet of every page, image, video, and PDF on your current site. Mark each as:

  • Keep: High-performing content that stays as-is
  • Update: Content with potential that needs refreshing
  • Consolidate: Thin pages that should merge into stronger ones
  • Remove: Outdated or irrelevant content

Point 6: Set a Realistic Budget and Timeline

Here is what contractor website redesigns actually cost in 2025:

Scope Cost Range Timeline Best For
Template refresh $3,000–$7,000 2–4 weeks New businesses, tight budgets
Custom redesign (10–20 pages) $8,000–$18,000 6–10 weeks Established businesses ready to scale
Full custom + SEO + content $20,000–$45,000 12–16 weeks Multi-location companies, aggressive growth goals

Point 7: Assemble Your Redesign Team

You need four roles minimum: a project manager, a designer who understands conversion optimization, a developer who knows local SEO, and a copywriter who can write for home service customers. One person can wear multiple hats, but do not expect a designer to also be your SEO strategist unless they have proven results.

Point 8: Choose the Right Platform

For home service businesses, we recommend WordPress with a lightweight theme or a custom build. Avoid Wix and Squarespace if SEO matters to you — their technical limitations cost you rankings. Webflow works for design flexibility but requires a developer for ongoing maintenance.

Point 9: Plan Your Content Architecture

Map every page your new site needs. A typical contractor site needs:

  • Homepage
  • Service pages (one per major service)
  • Service area / location pages (one per city you serve)
  • About page
  • Reviews / testimonials page
  • FAQ page
  • Blog (for SEO content)
  • Contact page

Point 10: Set Up Your Measurement Framework

Install Google Analytics 4, Google Search Console, and call tracking before launch. You cannot improve what you do not measure. Set up conversion goals for form submissions, phone clicks, and chat initiations.

Phase 2: Design (Points 11–20) — Converting Visitors Into Calls

Short answer: The design phase focuses on creating a mobile-first, conversion-optimized experience. Key elements include wireframing, visual hierarchy, trust signals, social proof placement, color psychology, typography for readability, image selection, navigation structure, CTA design, and form optimization. Every design decision should answer: "Does this make a visitor more likely to call?"

Design is where most redesigns go wrong. Designers focus on aesthetics. Contractors need conversions. The two are not mutually exclusive, but the priority must be clear: pretty does not pay the bills. Conversions do.

Point 11: Start With Mobile-First Wireframes

Over 65% of home service website traffic comes from mobile devices. Yet most designers still create desktop mockups first and adapt them to mobile as an afterthought. Reverse that. Design for the smallest screen first.

Mobile wireframes for contractors must prioritize:

  • Click-to-call button in the sticky header
  • One-tap quote request form
  • Service areas visible without scrolling
  • Reviews and trust signals above the fold

Point 12: Establish Clear Visual Hierarchy

Every page should guide the eye to one primary action. Use size, color, and spacing to create a clear path:

  1. Headline: What you do + where you do it ("Emergency Plumbing in Austin")
  2. Subheadline: Why choose you ("24/7 Service. Licensed & Insured. 4.9-Star Rating.")
  3. Primary CTA: The one action you want them to take
  4. Trust signals: Reviews, licenses, guarantees
  5. Secondary information: Service details, process explanation

Point 13: Place Trust Signals Strategically

Home service customers are letting strangers into their homes. Trust is the primary conversion barrier. Your website redesign checklist must include these trust elements:

Trust Signal Where to Place It Impact on Conversions
Google rating + review count Header, hero section, footer +15–25% form submissions
License & insurance badges Hero section, about page, footer +10–15% phone calls
Before/after project photos Service pages, gallery page +20–30% time on page
Money-back guarantee Near CTAs, pricing sections +12–18% quote requests
Years in business Header, about page, footer +8–12% trust signals

Point 14: Optimize Social Proof Placement

Reviews are not just for a testimonials page. Scatter them throughout your site. We have tested this extensively:

  • Homepage hero: "4.9 stars from 300+ Google reviews" next to your headline
  • Service pages: 2–3 relevant reviews specific to that service
  • Near CTAs: A review quote right above your "Get a Quote" button
  • Checkout/contact forms: A short testimonial reduces form abandonment

An HVAC client in Houston added review snippets to every service page CTA section. Their form submission rate increased 34% in 30 days.

Point 15: Use Color Psychology (But Do Not Overthink It)

Blue conveys trust. Orange and red create urgency. Green signals go/approval. These basics work, but the most important color rule for contractors is contrast. Your CTA button must stand out from everything else on the page. If your brand color is blue, do not use a blue CTA button on a blue background.

Point 16: Choose Readable Typography

Your customers are often over 45 and viewing your site on a phone. Use a minimum 16px font size for body text. Line height should be 1.5x the font size. Limit yourself to two font families — one for headings, one for body text.

Point 17: Select Real, High-Quality Images

Stock photos of smiling technicians kill credibility. Use real photos of your actual team, trucks, and completed projects. If you must use stock, choose images that look authentic — not overly polished. A slightly imperfect real photo outperforms a perfect stock photo every time.

Point 18: Design Intuitive Navigation

Your navigation should answer three questions in under 3 seconds:

  1. What services do you offer?
  2. Where do you work?
  3. How do I contact you?

Keep your main navigation to 5–7 items. Use dropdowns for service categories. Always include a prominent "Get a Quote" or "Call Now" button in the header.

Point 19: Design High-Contrast CTAs

Every page needs one primary CTA. Not three. Not five. One. Secondary actions (like "Learn More" or "View Services") should be visually subordinate. Your primary CTA button should:

  • Use a contrasting color
  • Be at least 44px tall on mobile (Apple's minimum touch target)
  • Use action-oriented text ("Get My Free Quote" beats "Submit")
  • Appear above the fold and repeat at the bottom of long pages

Point 20: Optimize Forms for Mobile

Every field you add to a form reduces completion rates. For a quote request, ask for:

  1. Name
  2. Phone number
  3. Service needed (dropdown)
  4. Zip code

That is it. Four fields. You can collect details during the follow-up call. One landscaping client reduced their form from 12 fields to 4 and saw quote requests increase 67%.

Phase 3: Development (Points 21–30) — Building for Speed, SEO, and Conversions

Short answer: The development phase turns designs into a functional website. Critical technical tasks include clean code, mobile responsiveness, page speed optimization, on-page SEO implementation, schema markup, SSL installation, analytics setup, form integration, call tracking, and cross-browser testing. Technical excellence directly impacts your Google rankings and conversion rates.

This is where the website redesign process gets technical. A beautiful design built on sloppy code will load slowly, rank poorly, and frustrate users. Here are the 10 development checkpoints every contractor redesign needs.

Point 21: Write Clean, Semantic HTML

Semantic HTML helps search engines understand your content structure. Use proper heading hierarchy (one H1 per page, H2s for sections, H3s for subsections). Use schema-appropriate tags like <article>, <section>, and <nav>. Avoid div soup — nested divs with no semantic meaning confuse crawlers and slow rendering.

Point 22: Ensure Perfect Mobile Responsiveness

Test on real devices, not just Chrome DevTools. Your site must function perfectly on:

  • iPhone (latest 3 models)
  • Samsung Galaxy (latest 3 models)
  • iPad and Android tablets

Pay special attention to tap targets. Buttons and links must be at least 44x44 pixels. Text must be readable without zooming. Forms must be completable with thumbs only.

Point 23: Optimize Page Speed Aggressively

Google uses page speed as a ranking factor. More importantly, 53% of mobile visitors abandon a site that takes longer than 3 seconds to load (Google/SOASTA research, 2023). Your website redesign checklist must include these speed optimizations:

Optimization Expected Impact How to Implement
Image compression 30–60% faster load Use WebP format, compress to 80% quality, lazy load below-fold images
Minify CSS/JS 10–20% faster load Remove whitespace, comments, unused code
Enable browser caching 50%+ faster repeat visits Set cache headers for static assets
Use a CDN 20–40% faster global load Cloudflare, BunnyCDN, or StackPath
Defer non-critical JavaScript 1–2 second faster First Contentful Paint Add defer or async attributes to script tags

Point 24: Implement On-Page SEO for Every Page

Every page needs unique, optimized metadata:

  • Title tag: 50–60 characters, include primary keyword + location
  • Meta description: 150–160 characters, include a call to action
  • H1: One per page, includes primary keyword naturally
  • URL: Short, descriptive, includes keyword if possible
  • Image alt text: Descriptive, includes keywords where relevant
  • Internal links: 2–3 per page linking to related content

Point 25: Add Local Business Schema Markup

Schema markup helps Google display rich results for your business. At minimum, implement:

  • LocalBusiness schema with name, address, phone, hours, and service area
  • Service schema for each service page
  • Review schema (if using aggregate ratings)
  • BreadcrumbList schema for navigation
  • FAQ schema for FAQ sections (can earn rich snippets)

A plumbing company in Denver added LocalBusiness and FAQ schema. Their FAQ pages started appearing in Google's "People Also Ask" boxes, increasing organic traffic 45% in 60 days.

Point 26: Install SSL Certificate (HTTPS)

HTTPS is mandatory. Google marks non-HTTPS sites as "Not Secure" in Chrome. Most hosting providers offer free SSL certificates through Let's Encrypt. Ensure all resources (images, scripts, CSS) load over HTTPS to avoid mixed content warnings.

Point 27: Set Up Analytics and Tracking

Before launch, verify these are working:

  1. Google Analytics 4 property configured
  2. Google Search Console verified
  3. Call tracking numbers installed (CallRail, CallTrackingMetrics, or similar)
  4. Form submission events tracked in GA4
  5. Google Ads conversion tracking (if running ads)
  6. Facebook Pixel (if running social ads)

Point 28: Integrate Forms With Your CRM

Form submissions should flow directly into your CRM or scheduling system. Popular integrations for contractors include:

  • ServiceTitan
  • Housecall Pro
  • Jobber
  • FieldPulse
  • Zapier (connects almost anything)

Manual data entry from email notifications costs you 15–30 minutes per lead and introduces errors. Automation pays for itself within weeks.

Point 29: Implement Call Tracking

You cannot optimize what you do not measure. Dynamic number insertion (DNI) shows different phone numbers to visitors from different sources (organic, Google Ads, Facebook, direct). This tells you exactly which marketing channels drive calls. Without call tracking, you are guessing.

Point 30: Test Across Browsers and Devices

Test your site on Chrome, Safari, Firefox, and Edge. Test on iOS Safari and Android Chrome. Check:

  • All forms submit correctly
  • Phone numbers are clickable on mobile
  • Images load properly
  • CTA buttons are tappable
  • No console errors
  • Print styles work (some customers print service pages)

Phase 4: Launch (Points 31–35) — Going Live Without Breaking Anything

Short answer: The launch phase involves pre-launch testing, URL redirect mapping, DNS cutover, post-launch verification, and stakeholder communication. A proper website launch checklist prevents traffic loss, ranking drops, and broken functionality. Never launch on a Friday afternoon — give yourself 2–3 business days to catch and fix issues.

Launch day is stressful. But with proper preparation, it should be boring. Boring means nothing broke. Here is your 5-point launch protocol.

Point 31: Complete Pre-Launch Testing

Run through this checklist 48 hours before launch:

  • All pages load without errors
  • All links work (use a tool like Screaming Frog)
  • All forms submit and notifications arrive
  • Phone numbers click-to-call on mobile
  • Images have alt text
  • No placeholder content remains ("Lorem ipsum," "Coming Soon")
  • Robots.txt allows indexing
  • XML sitemap is generated and submitted to Search Console
  • 301 redirects are mapped for every changed URL
  • SSL certificate is active

Point 32: Map and Implement 301 Redirects

This is the single most important technical step in any redesign. When URLs change, you must redirect the old URL to the new one with a 301 (permanent) redirect. Without redirects:

  • Visitors bookmarking old pages get 404 errors
  • Google removes old pages from its index
  • Backlinks to old pages stop passing SEO value
  • Your rankings tank

Create a redirect map in a spreadsheet. Old URL in column A, new URL in column B. Test every redirect before and after launch. One missed redirect can cost you a page 1 ranking.

Point 33: Execute the DNS Cutover

When you are ready to go live:

  1. Update DNS records to point to the new server
  2. Wait for propagation (usually 1–24 hours)
  3. Test the live site immediately after DNS updates
  4. Keep the old site accessible on a staging URL for 30 days

Pro tip: Lower your DNS TTL (Time To Live) to 300 seconds 24 hours before launch. This speeds up propagation.

Point 34: Conduct Post-Launch Verification

Within 2 hours of launch, verify:

  • Homepage loads correctly
  • All critical pages load (services, contact, about)
  • Forms submit and you receive notifications
  • Click-to-call works on mobile
  • Google Analytics is recording traffic
  • Search Console shows no crawl errors
  • Social sharing previews display correctly (use Facebook Debugger and Twitter Card Validator)

Point 35: Communicate With Stakeholders

Notify your team, your agency partners, and any vendors who link to your site. Update your:

  • Google Business Profile with new URL if it changed
  • Social media profiles
  • Email signatures
  • Directory listings (Yelp, Angi, HomeAdvisor, BBB)
  • PPC landing page URLs if they changed

Phase 5: Post-Launch (Points 36–40) — Optimizing for Long-Term Growth

Short answer: Post-launch optimization includes monitoring analytics, fixing crawl errors, A/B testing key pages, gathering user feedback, and building a content calendar. The work does not end at launch — it begins. The contractors who treat launch as day one of optimization outperform those who set it and forget it.

Most agencies hand over the keys and disappear. That is when the real work starts. Here is your post-launch optimization protocol.

Point 36: Monitor Analytics Daily for 30 Days

Watch these metrics closely after launch:

Metric What to Watch For Red Flag
Organic traffic Gradual increase or stable baseline 20%+ drop in first 2 weeks
Bounce rate Below 60% for service pages Above 75% consistently
Conversion rate 2–5% for home service sites Below 1% after 2 weeks
Page load time Under 3 seconds on mobile Above 5 seconds
404 errors Zero or minimal Spike in Search Console

Point 37: Fix Crawl Errors Immediately

Check Google Search Console daily for the first two weeks. Fix any crawl errors, coverage issues, or mobile usability problems within 24 hours of discovery. A crawl error on your contact page can cost you leads for days.

Point 38: A/B Test Your Highest-Traffic Pages

Once your site is stable, start testing. Focus on:

  • Headline variations on your homepage
  • CTA button color and text
  • Form length and field order
  • Hero image (team photo vs. project photo vs. truck photo)
  • Social proof placement

One roofing client tested "Get a Free Quote" vs. "Get My Free Estimate" on their primary CTA. The second version increased clicks 22%. Small changes compound.

Point 39: Gather User Feedback

Ask actual customers about your new site. Send a 2-question survey:

  1. "What made you choose to contact us?" (open-ended)
  2. "Was there anything on our website that was confusing or missing?" (open-ended)

Customer feedback reveals blind spots. One HVAC company discovered customers wanted to see pricing ranges, not just "call for a quote." They added estimated price ranges to service pages and saw quote requests increase 28%.

Point 40: Build a 90-Day Content Calendar

Fresh content signals to Google that your site is active and authoritative. Plan content around:

  • Seasonal topics: "Preparing Your AC for Summer" in March, "Winterizing Your Plumbing" in October
  • Service-specific guides: Deep dives into each service you offer
  • Location-based content: "Best HVAC Systems for [City] Homes"
  • Customer questions: Answer every question your team hears on service calls

Aim for 2–4 new pieces of content per month. Quality over quantity. One comprehensive 2,500-word guide outperforms ten 300-word posts.

Common Mistakes to Avoid During Your Website Redesign

We have seen contractors make the same mistakes repeatedly. Avoid these, and you are already ahead of 80% of your competitors.

Mistake 1: Redesigning Without a Goal

"Our site looks old" is not a business goal. Every redesign decision should tie back to a measurable outcome. If you cannot explain how a design element increases leads or rankings, question whether you need it.

Mistake 2: Ignoring Mobile Experience

We still see contractor sites where the mobile menu is broken, phone numbers are not clickable, and forms require pinch-zooming. In 2025, this is inexcusable. Google indexes mobile-first. Your customers browse mobile-first. Design mobile-first.

Mistake 3: Deleting High-Performing Content

That old blog post ranking #3 for "emergency plumber near me"? It is worth more than your new homepage design. Never delete content without checking its traffic and rankings first. Update it, improve it, redirect it — but do not blindly delete during a redesign.

Mistake 4: Using a Generic Designer

A designer who built e-commerce sites for fashion brands does not understand home service conversion psychology. They do not know that trust signals matter more than aesthetics. They do not know that phone calls matter more than email signups. Hire someone who has built contractor websites before.

Mistake 5: Launching Without Testing

We have seen sites launch with broken contact forms, 404 homepages, and "Lorem ipsum" still in the footer. Create a pre-launch checklist and check every item. Then have someone else check it. Then check it again.

Mistake 6: Forgetting About Local SEO

Home service businesses live and die by local search. Your redesign must include location pages, local schema, NAP consistency (Name, Address, Phone), and Google Business Profile optimization. A beautiful site that does not rank in local search is a billboard in the desert.

Mistake 7: Setting It and Forgetting It

A website is not a brochure. It is a living marketing asset. The contractors who win online are the ones who publish content monthly, test CTAs quarterly, and update their site annually. Your redesign is the starting line, not the finish line.

Mistake 8: Not Tracking Conversions

We ask every new client: "How many leads did your website generate last month?" Most do not know. Without call tracking, form analytics, and goal tracking in GA4, you are flying blind. Install tracking before launch. Review it weekly.

Frequently Asked Questions About Contractor Website Redesigns

How long does a contractor website redesign take?

A typical contractor website redesign takes 6–12 weeks from kickoff to launch. Simple template-based refreshes can be done in 2–4 weeks. Full custom redesigns with SEO and content strategy take 12–16 weeks. The planning phase usually takes 2–3 weeks, design 2–4 weeks, development 3–6 weeks, and launch 1 week.

How much should a contractor website redesign cost?

Expect to invest $8,000–$25,000 for a professional contractor website redesign in 2025. Template-based sites start around $3,000–$7,000. Custom designs with local SEO, content strategy, and conversion optimization range from $15,000–$45,000. The ROI on a well-executed redesign typically pays for itself within 6–12 months through increased leads.

Will a redesign hurt my Google rankings?

A redesign can hurt rankings if done incorrectly — especially if URLs change without 301 redirects, content is deleted, or page speed worsens. However, a properly executed redesign with SEO preservation should maintain or improve rankings within 4–8 weeks. The key is working with a team that understands technical SEO.

Should I redesign my website or just update it?

Update if your site is less than 3 years old, mobile-friendly, and generating leads. Redesign if your site is over 4 years old, not mobile-responsive, loads slowly, has broken functionality, or is not converting visitors. A good rule: if you are embarrassed to send potential customers to your site, it is time for a redesign.

What platform is best for contractor websites?

WordPress is the best platform for most contractor websites due to its SEO flexibility, plugin ecosystem, and scalability. Custom builds work for larger companies with dedicated developers. Avoid Wix and Squarespace if organic search is a priority — their technical SEO limitations will cost you rankings over time.

How do I keep my SEO rankings during a redesign?

Preserve rankings by: (1) auditing current rankings and traffic before starting, (2) maintaining or improving URL structure, (3) implementing 301 redirects for every changed URL, (4) keeping high-performing content, (5) maintaining page speed or improving it, (6) preserving title tags and meta descriptions, and (7) submitting the new sitemap to Google immediately after launch.

What pages does a contractor website need?

Every contractor website needs: homepage, individual service pages for each major service, service area/location pages for each city served, about page, reviews/testimonials page, FAQ page, contact page, and a blog for SEO content. Multi-service contractors typically need 15–30 pages minimum.

How do I measure the success of my redesign?

Track these metrics: organic traffic (should increase 20–40% within 6 months), conversion rate (form submissions + calls divided by total visitors), cost per lead (total marketing spend divided by leads), average session duration, bounce rate, keyword rankings for target terms, and total leads generated per month. Compare pre-launch and post-launch numbers monthly.

How often should I redesign my contractor website?

Plan a full redesign every 3–4 years. Technology, design trends, and user expectations change rapidly. Between redesigns, update content monthly, refresh imagery annually, and make continuous improvements based on analytics and user feedback. Think of your website like a truck — regular maintenance prevents major overhauls.

Can I redesign my website myself?

You can, but most contractors should not. A DIY redesign using a page builder might save $5,000–$10,000 upfront but typically costs far more in lost leads, poor SEO, and time spent troubleshooting. Your time is worth $100–$300+ per hour on service calls. Spending 100+ hours on a website redesign that generates mediocre results is poor ROI. Hire professionals who do this daily.

What is the biggest mistake contractors make during redesigns?

The biggest mistake is focusing on aesthetics over conversions. Contractors get excited about a new look but neglect the elements that actually drive calls: clear CTAs, trust signals, mobile optimization, fast load times, and local SEO. A beautiful site that does not generate leads is an expensive decoration.

How do I choose a web design agency for my contracting business?

Look for: (1) a portfolio of contractor or home service websites, (2) case studies showing lead generation results, (3) understanding of local SEO, (4) transparent pricing and timelines, (5) a defined process with clear milestones, and (6) ongoing support after launch. Ask for references from contractor clients and call them.

Should my redesign include a blog?

Yes, if you are committed to publishing 2–4 quality posts per month. A blog is one of the most effective SEO tools for contractors. It drives organic traffic, builds authority, and answers customer questions. However, a blog with three posts from 2019 hurts more than it helps. If you will not maintain it, skip it and focus on optimizing your service pages.

What is the difference between a website refresh and a redesign?

A refresh updates visual elements — colors, fonts, images, and minor layout changes — while keeping the existing structure and platform. A redesign rebuilds the site from the ground up, often changing platforms, URL structures, content architecture, and functionality. Refresh when the foundation is solid. Redesign when the foundation is cracked.

How do I prepare my team for a website redesign?

Assign one internal project manager as the point of contact. Gather all brand assets (logos, photos, videos, licenses, insurance docs). Document your service offerings, service areas, and pricing. Collect customer testimonials and project photos. Define your goals and success metrics. Block time for reviews and feedback. The more prepared you are, the faster and cheaper the redesign.
